sections.h2: What is a transfer on death deed in Wisconsin?
sections.html:
It is a recorded document that names who receives a piece of Wisconsin real estate when the owner dies, with no probate case needed for that property. The law behind it is Wis. Stat. 705.15, which describes a "TOD beneficiary designation" made on a recorded document. People call it a transfer on death deed, and the register of deeds treats it as one.

Five kinds of ownership can use it:

  • An interest held by one individual and by no one else
  • A fractional interest held as a tenant in common
  • An interest held by a spouse as marital property
  • An interest held by spouses as survivorship marital property
  • An interest held by two or more people as joint tenants

The transfer happens on the death of the sole owner, or of the last of several owners to die. Until then the beneficiary owns nothing.

The document has to name the owner or owners, name the beneficiary, and state that the transfer takes effect only on the owner's death. For marital property held by a spouse, both spouses with an interest must sign. Section 705.15(2)(a) lays out these requirements.

The wording is flexible. An owner can write "transfer on death" or "pay on death," or use the letters TOD or POD, placed after the owner's name and ahead of the beneficiary's name. Primary beneficiaries can be listed along with contingent ones, who take if a primary beneficiary does not survive. The designation can go on the original deed that gave the owner title, or on a later document signed and recorded by the sole owner or by all surviving owners.

Capacity matters. The mental capacity needed to sign or cancel a designation is the same as the capacity needed to make or revoke a will under s. 853.01.

Recording is what makes the document work. A designation is ineffective unless the document and the recording fees reach the register of deeds in the county where the land sits before the sole or last owner dies. A signed paper in a drawer does nothing.

sections.h2: Can the owner still sell or change the plan after signing?
sections.html:
Yes. Under section 705.15(3)(a), a designation does not affect ownership until the sole or last owner dies, even if the document says otherwise. The owner keeps full control, and subsection (3)(c) adds that the rule does not limit a transfer made during the owner's life. A sale, a gift or a mortgage during life is still possible.

To cancel or change a designation, the owner records a new instrument. It has to meet every one of these tests:

  • It is a new designation document, an instrument of revocation, or a lifetime deed that expressly revokes the earlier recorded document, in whole or in part
  • The owner acknowledged it after acknowledging the earlier document
  • It reaches the register of deeds in the property's county before the sole or last owner dies

When several owners signed one designation, one owner's revocation does not undo the designation for another owner's interest. For joint tenants or spouses with survivorship marital property, the designation is revoked only if all living joint tenants or spouses revoke it.

sections.h2: What happens to the house when the owner dies
sections.html:
Ownership passes to the surviving beneficiaries, subject to any lien or encumbrance on the property. If a named beneficiary died first, that beneficiary's issue who would take under s. 854.06(3) step in. If nobody qualifies, the interest goes to the deceased owner's estate. Chapter 854 applies to these transfers.

The beneficiary then needs paper proof of title. Section 705.15(5) points to three routes: s. 863.27, s. 865.201 or s. 867.046. The last one runs through the register of deeds. The beneficiary files a signed, sworn application with the decedent's name, residence and address, the applicant's details and the date of death. For real estate the applicant adds the most recent property tax bill, a legal description and a copy of the deed that created the TOD interest. Once recorded, the application ends the decedent's interest with the same force as an order from the probate court of the decedent's home county.

Three timing rules matter:

  • If the beneficiary or personal representative has not started a confirmation within 90 days of death, any interested person may apply under s. 867.046(2m).
  • A claim to recover real property that went to a TOD beneficiary is barred unless a complaint and a lis pendens are filed within 120 days after the death (s. 705.15(8)).
  • A good-faith buyer or lender who deals with the petitioner takes title free of claims by the decedent's estate (s. 867.046(6)).

Recording costs $30 per document under s. 59.43(2)(ag), and the register may refuse a document that misses its format rules. Those rules include a blank 3-inch by 3-inch space in the upper right corner of page one, the drafter's name, a legal description, no Social Security number, and a parcel identification number in counties that require one.

The state real estate transfer fee does not apply. Under s. 77.25(10m), a conveyance made solely to designate a TOD beneficiary is exempt, and under s. 77.25(11m) so is the nonprobate transfer at death. When removing a decedent's interest, the filer submits a Real Estate Transfer Return in My Tax Account, picks "Termination of Decedent's Interest," and claims exemption 11m if a TOD document was recorded before death. The filer enters the recorded document number and an estimated value taken from the most recent tax bill. Questions go to the Department of Revenue at RETR@wisconsin.gov or (608) 264-6885.

sections.h2: Selling the house as a beneficiary
sections.html:
A beneficiary can sell once the interest is confirmed and any liens are dealt with. The property passes subject to liens, so a mortgage or tax debt does not vanish at death. It stays on the title until paid, which makes a payoff figure the first thing to ask a title company for.

A beneficiary who lives far away or inherits a house that needs repairs may want to sell quickly. Line up the confirmation paperwork first: the register of deeds application, the recent tax bill and the recorded designation. A cash buyer can often close without the owner making repairs, but the title still has to be confirmed in your name before closing.

If the estate has an open informal administration, the Wisconsin court system offers form PR-1827, a statement of termination or confirmation of interests in property tied to ss. 705.15, 865.20 and 865.201. An attorney or personal representative completes it, and a certified copy or duplicate original may be recorded with the register of deeds.

A rough path to closing: gather the recorded designation and a death certificate, file the application with the register of deeds, record the confirmation, get a payoff figure for any mortgage or tax debt, and then sign the sale contract. An attorney can say which path suits a particular family.

faqs.q: Does a Wisconsin transfer on death deed avoid probate?
faqs.a: Yes, for the property named in it. Section 705.15 lets the property pass to the designated beneficiary without probate, but only if the designation was recorded with the register of deeds before the last owner died. Other assets without a beneficiary can still need a probate case.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to consent to the designation?
faqs.a: No. The owner signs, and both spouses sign for marital property, but no beneficiary signature is required. The owner can revoke the designation by recording a new instrument without involving the beneficiary.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a TOD designation in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: The register of deeds charges $30 per recorded document under s. 59.43(2)(ag). The state transfer fee does not apply because s. 77.25(10m) exempts a conveyance made solely to designate a TOD beneficiary. Call the register of deeds in the property's county about local recording requirements.

faqs.q: What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?
faqs.a: The property goes to the predeceased beneficiary's issue who would take under s. 854.06(3). If no beneficiary or qualifying issue survives all owners, it passes to the estate of the sole or last owner. A contingent beneficiary named in the document takes before that point.

faqs.q: Can the owner still sell the house after naming a beneficiary?
faqs.a: Yes. The designation does not change ownership until death, and s. 705.15(3)(c) leaves lifetime transfers untouched. A sale during life ends the owner's interest, so nothing is left for the designation to pass at death. Ask an attorney before signing a deed.
